title: Νέφος ἀνδρῶν
titleEn: The Battle-Order of Nestor and the Rebuke of Odysseus — Iliad 4.272–363
part: The Battle-Order of Nestor and the Rebuke of Odysseus (4.272–363)
about: Agamemnon goes on along the ranks. At the two Ajaxes the poet likens their dark, bristling battle-lines to a storm-cloud that a goatherd sees coming over the sea, and Agamemnon, glad, tells them he need not urge them, and wishes that all had their heart. At Nestor he finds the old man marshalling the Pylians: horsemen in front, foot-soldiers behind, the weak in the middle, with orders for the charioteers to keep their places and thrust from their cars. Agamemnon wishes Nestor had back the strength of his knees, and Nestor answers that the gods do not give everything at once, but that he will still advise. Further on, Menestheus and Odysseus stand waiting with their men, and Agamemnon reviles them for hanging back. Odysseus answers with a scowl; Agamemnon smiles and takes back his words.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, Ἀτρεΐδης δὲ παρῴχετο γηθόσυνος κῆρ·
ἦλθε δ’ ἐπ’ Αἰάντεσσι κιὼν ἀνὰ οὐλαμὸν ἀνδρῶν·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and Atreus’-son went past, glad in heart;
and he came to the Ajaxes, going up through the crowd of men;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the son of Atreus passed on, glad at heart; and, moving through the crowd of men, he came to the Ajaxes;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ ‘so he spoke’ closes Idomeneus’ speech from the last part, and Ἀτρεΐδης ‘son of Atreus’ is Agamemnon, who now goes on along the ranks. παρῴχετο is the imperfect of παροίχομαι ‘go past’, and γηθόσυνος ‘glad’ takes κῆρ ‘in heart’, an accusative of respect. Αἰάντεσσι is the epic dative plural of Αἴας: the two Ajaxes, who are named together as the dual τώ in the next line. κιών is the present participle of κίω ‘go’, taken with ἀνά ‘up through’ and οὐλαμόν ‘crowd’, a rare word. A new paragraph begins at 272.

sentences.t: τὼ δὲ κορυσσέσθην, ἅμα δὲ νέφος εἵπετο πεζῶν.
sentences.l: and the two were arming themselves, and together with them a cloud followed, of foot-soldiers.
sentences.i: The two were arming themselves, and a cloud of foot-soldiers followed with them.
sentences.n: τώ is the dual of the article used as a pronoun, ‘the two’: the two Ajaxes. κορυσσέσθην is a dual imperfect middle of κορύσσω ‘arm’ (from κόρυς ‘helmet’), ‘were arming themselves’. ἅμα ‘together’ goes with εἵπετο, the imperfect of ἕπομαι ‘follow’ in its augmented form. νέφος … πεζῶν ‘a cloud of foot-soldiers’ already sets up the simile that follows: a mass of men seen as a cloud.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἀπὸ σκοπιῆς εἶδεν νέφος αἰπόλος ἀνὴρ
ἐρχόμενον κατὰ πόντον ὑπὸ Ζεφύροιο ἰωῆς·
sentences.l:
And as when from a lookout a goatherd man saw a cloud
coming over the sea beneath the blast of the West Wind;
sentences.i: As when a goatherd, from a lookout, sees a cloud coming over the sea under the blast of the West Wind;
sentences.n: A simile begins with ὡς δ’ ὅτε ‘and as when’ and runs to 279; its other half, τοῖαι ‘such’, comes at 280. εἶδεν and the later ἤλασε are past tenses used for what happens whenever it happens, so English gives them in the present. αἰπόλος ἀνήρ is ‘a goatherd man’, and ἀπὸ σκοπιῆς ‘from a lookout’ is a place for watching. νέφος ‘cloud’ is the object and ἐρχόμενον ‘coming’ agrees with it. ὑπὸ Ζεφύροιο ἰωῆς gives the cause: ὑπό with the genitive, ‘under the force of’, ἰωή ‘blast’, and Ζέφυρος the West Wind.

sentences.t:
τῷ δέ τ’ ἄνευθεν ἐόντι μελάντερον ἠΰτε πίσσα
φαίνετ’ ἰὸν κατὰ πόντον, ἄγει δέ τε λαίλαπα πολλήν,
sentences.l:
and to him, being far off, blacker, like pitch,
it appears, going over the sea, and it brings a great squall,
sentences.i: and to him, far off as he is, it looks blacker than pitch as it moves over the sea, and it brings a great squall,
sentences.n: τῷ … ἐόντι ‘to him, being’ is the goatherd again, with ἄνευθεν ‘far off’. From that distance the cloud looks μελάντερον ‘blacker’, and ἠΰτε πίσσα ‘like pitch’ gives the measure, so English says ‘blacker than pitch’. φαίνετ’ is φαίνεται ‘appears’, with ἰόν ‘going’ (from εἶμι) and κατὰ πόντον ‘over the sea’. The particle τε in δέ τε is common in similes and marks what is always so. λαίλαπα πολλήν ‘a great squall’ is what the cloud brings with it.

sentences.t: ῥίγησέν τε ἰδών, ὑπό τε σπέος ἤλασε μῆλα·
sentences.l: and he shuddered, having seen it, and under a cave drove his flocks;
sentences.i: and he shudders when he sees it and drives his flocks in under the shelter of a cave;
sentences.n: ῥίγησε is the aorist of ῥιγέω ‘shudder’, and the participle ἰδών ‘having seen’ gives the cause. τε … τε joins the two things the goatherd does. ὑπό with the accusative σπέος ‘cave’ means ‘in under’, because the flocks are driven there. ἤλασε is the aorist of ἐλαύνω ‘drive’, and μῆλα is the flock, sheep and goats together. The aorists are general, so English again uses the present.

sentences.t:
τοῖαι ἅμ’ Αἰάντεσσι διοτρεφέων αἰζηῶν
δήϊον ἐς πόλεμον πυκιναὶ κίνυντο φάλαγγες
κυάνεαι, σάκεσίν τε καὶ ἔγχεσι πεφρικυῖαι.
sentences.l:
Such, with the Ajaxes, of Zeus-nurtured young men
into hostile war moved the thick battle-lines,
dark, bristling with shields and with spears.
sentences.i: Such were the thick, dark battle-lines of Zeus-nurtured young men that moved with the Ajaxes into hostile war, bristling with shields and spears.
sentences.n: τοῖαι ‘such’ completes the simile begun at 275: the goatherd’s storm-cloud is matched by the Ajaxes’ ranks, and the match is their darkness, κυάνεαι ‘dark’. ἅμ’ Αἰάντεσσι ‘with the Ajaxes’ takes the dative; διοτρεφέων αἰζηῶν ‘of Zeus-nurtured young men’ (αἰζηός is a vigorous young man) says whose battle-lines they are. δήϊον ‘hostile’ goes with πόλεμον, and πυκιναί ‘thick’ with φάλαγγες ‘battle-lines’. πεφρικυῖαι is a perfect participle of φρίσσω ‘bristle’, with σάκεσιν ‘shields’ and ἔγχεσι ‘spears’ for what they bristle with.

sentences.t:
καὶ τοὺς μὲν γήθησεν ἰδὼν κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων,
καί σφεας φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
And at them rejoiced, seeing, lord Agamemnon,
and, lifting his voice, to them winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: Lord Agamemnon rejoiced when he saw them, and lifting his voice he spoke winged words to them:
sentences.n: The objects are the Ajaxes and their men: τοὺς μέν ‘them’ (the article as a pronoun), with γήθησεν ‘rejoiced’ (aorist of γηθέω) and the participle ἰδών ‘seeing’. κρείων ‘lord’ is the word of rank for Agamemnon here. The second line is a stock line: σφεας is the epic accusative plural ‘them’, φωνήσας ‘lifting his voice’, and ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα ‘he spoke winged words to them’. Agamemnon’s speech follows.

sentences.t:
Αἴαντ’ Ἀργείων ἡγήτορε χαλκοχιτώνων,
σφῶϊ μέν· οὐ γὰρ ἔοικ’ ὀτρυνέμεν· οὔ τι κελεύω·
sentences.l:
“Ajaxes, two leaders of the bronze-shirted Argives,
you two, on the one hand — for it is not fitting to urge — not at all do I order;
sentences.i: “Ajaxes, you two leaders of the bronze-shirted Argives: as for you two — for it is not fitting to urge you on — I give no orders at all;
sentences.n: Αἴαντ’ (Αἴαντε) and ἡγήτορε are dual vocatives, ‘Ajaxes’ and ‘two leaders’, and σφῶϊ is the dual pronoun ‘you two’; χαλκοχιτώνων ‘bronze-shirted’ is a stock epithet. μέν marks a contrast with the others whom Agamemnon has still to rouse. οὐ γὰρ ἔοικ’ ὀτρυνέμεν gives the reason for saying nothing: ἔοικε ‘it is fitting’ governs the epic infinitive ὀτρυνέμεν ‘to urge’. κελεύω ‘I order’ is a different verb from ὀτρύνω ‘urge’, and the English keeps them apart.

sentences.t: αὐτὼ γὰρ μάλα λαὸν ἀνώγετον ἶφι μάχεσθαι.
sentences.l: for you two yourselves very much bid the people to fight with force.
sentences.i: for you two yourselves most earnestly bid the army to fight powerfully.
sentences.n: αὐτώ is the dual of αὐτός, ‘you two yourselves’, taking up σφῶϊ. ἀνώγετον is a dual of ἄνωγα, a perfect with present sense, ‘I bid’; λαόν ‘people’ is its object and μάχεσθαι ‘to fight’ the thing bidden. ἶφι ‘with force’ is an old adverb, and μάλα ‘very much’ strengthens the verb. The reason for leaving the Ajaxes alone is that they already do the urging themselves.

sentences.t:
αἲ γὰρ Ζεῦ τε πάτερ καὶ Ἀθηναίη καὶ Ἄπολλον
τοῖος πᾶσιν θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσι γένοιτο·
τώ κε τάχ’ ἠμύσειε πόλις Πριάμοιο ἄνακτος
χερσὶν ὑφ’ ἡμετέρῃσιν ἁλοῦσά τε περθομένη τε.
sentences.l:
Would that — Father Zeus, and Athena, and Apollo —
such a heart for all in their chests might come to be;
then soon would the city of lord Priam bow down,
beneath our hands taken and being sacked.”
sentences.i: If only — Father Zeus, Athena, and Apollo — all had such a heart in their breasts; then the city of lord Priam would soon fall, taken and sacked beneath our hands.”
sentences.n: αἲ γὰρ … γένοιτο is a wish (αἲ γάρ ‘would that’ with the optative), with the three gods called on in between as vocatives. τοῖος ‘such’ points back to the Ajaxes’ spirit, and θυμός ‘heart’ is courage. τώ κε … ἠμύσειε ‘then would … bow down’ is the result, with ἠμύω ‘sink down’ said of a city; χερσὶν ὑφ’ ἡμετέρῃσιν is ‘beneath our hands’, and ἁλοῦσα ‘taken’ (aorist participle of ἁλίσκομαι) and περθομένη ‘sacked’ agree with πόλις. The same words stand in Agamemnon’s wish at 2.371–374, with a different line between.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν τοὺς μὲν λίπεν αὐτοῦ, βῆ δὲ μετ’ ἄλλους·
sentences.l: So having spoken, those he left on the spot, and went among others;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and left them there, and went on to others;
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών ‘so having spoken’ is a common line-opener. The pair τοὺς μέν … βῆ δέ sets the Ajaxes, left behind, against ἄλλους ‘others’, whom he goes on to (μετά with the accusative). λίπεν is the unaugmented aorist of λείπω, and αὐτοῦ is an adverb, ‘on the spot, right there’. A new paragraph begins at 292.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ὅ γε Νέστορ’ ἔτετμε λιγὺν Πυλίων ἀγορητὴν
οὓς ἑτάρους στέλλοντα καὶ ὀτρύνοντα μάχεσθαι
ἀμφὶ μέγαν Πελάγοντα Ἀλάστορά τε Χρομίον τε
Αἵμονά τε κρείοντα Βίαντά τε ποιμένα λαῶν·
sentences.l:
There he came upon Nestor, the clear-voiced speaker of the Pylians,
marshalling his own companions and urging them to fight
around great Pelagon and Alastor and Chromius
and lord Haemon and Bias, shepherd of the people;
sentences.i: There he found Nestor, the clear-voiced speaker of the Pylians, marshalling his companions and urging them to fight around great Pelagon, Alastor, Chromius, lord Haemon, and Bias, shepherd of the people;
sentences.n: ἔνθ’ ὅ γε ‘there he’ brings Agamemnon to the next group. ἔτετμε is an aorist of an old verb meaning ‘came upon, found’. λιγύς ‘clear-voiced’ and ἀγορητής ‘speaker’ are Nestor’s stock description (as at 1.248). οὓς ἑτάρους ‘his own companions’ uses ὅς as the possessive ‘his own’, not the relative. στέλλοντα and ὀτρύνοντα are present participles, ‘marshalling’ and ‘urging on’, and ἀμφί with the accusative names the men round whom he gathers them: Pelagon, Alastor, Chromius, Haemon and Bias. κρείοντα ‘lord’ goes with Haemon, and ποιμένα λαῶν ‘shepherd of the people’ with Bias.

sentences.t:
ἱππῆας μὲν πρῶτα σὺν ἵπποισιν καὶ ὄχεσφι,
πεζοὺς δ’ ἐξόπιθε στῆσεν πολέας τε καὶ ἐσθλοὺς
ἕρκος ἔμεν πολέμοιο·
sentences.i: He set the horsemen first, with their horses and chariots, and the foot-soldiers behind, many and good, to be a bulwark against war;
sentences.n: μέν … δέ sets the horsemen (ἱππῆας) against the foot-soldiers (πεζούς): Nestor gives each kind of fighter its place. πρῶτα ‘first’ is an adverb, and ὄχεσφι is the dative plural in -φι, ‘with chariots’. ἐξόπιθε ‘behind’ and στῆσεν ‘stationed’ (aorist of ἵστημι) put the foot-soldiers at the back, πολέας τε καὶ ἐσθλούς ‘many and good’, ἕρκος ἔμεν ‘to be a fence’ (ἔμεν is the epic infinitive of εἰμί). The genitive πολέμοιο is what they fence against, as at 1.284.

sentences.t:
κακοὺς δ’ ἐς μέσσον ἔλασσεν,
ὄφρα καὶ οὐκ ἐθέλων τις ἀναγκαίῃ πολεμίζοι.
sentences.l:
but the base he drove into the middle,
so that even one not willing, by compulsion, might fight.
sentences.i: but the base he drove into the middle, so that even a man who was unwilling would fight under compulsion.
sentences.n: κακούς here are men who are ‘base’ in battle, the cowards, set against the ἐσθλούς ‘good’ of 298. ἐς μέσσον ‘into the middle’ shows the plan: the weak are boxed in between horse and foot. ἔλασσεν is the aorist of ἐλαύνω ‘drive’, with doubled σ. ὄφρα takes the optative πολεμίζοι ‘might fight’, a purpose clause; καὶ οὐκ ἐθέλων τις is ‘even someone not willing’, and ἀναγκαίῃ ‘by necessity’ is the dative of ἀναγκαίη, a form of ἀνάγκη.

sentences.t:
ἱππεῦσιν μὲν πρῶτ’ ἐπετέλλετο· τοὺς γὰρ ἀνώγει
σφοὺς ἵππους ἐχέμεν μηδὲ κλονέεσθαι ὁμίλῳ·
sentences.l:
To the horsemen first he laid his charge; for them he bade
hold their own horses, and not be thrown into confusion in the throng;
sentences.i: To the horsemen he gave his charge first, for he bade them hold their horses in check and not be thrown into confusion in the throng;
sentences.n: ἱππεῦσιν ‘to the horsemen’ takes up the first half of the list at 297, with ἐπετέλλετο ‘he laid a charge’ (imperfect of ἐπιτέλλομαι). τοὺς γὰρ ἀνώγει explains: ἀνώγει is the imperfect of ἄνωγα ‘bid’, and τούς, the article as a pronoun, is ‘them’. The infinitives ἐχέμεν (epic for ἔχειν) ‘to hold’ and κλονέεσθαι ‘to be thrown into confusion’ (passive of κλονέω, ‘drive in confusion’) say what is bidden; σφούς is ‘their own’, and ὁμίλῳ ‘in the throng’ is a bare dative of place.

sentences.t:
μηδέ τις ἱπποσύνῃ τε καὶ ἠνορέηφι πεποιθὼς
οἶος πρόσθ’ ἄλλων μεμάτω Τρώεσσι μάχεσθαι,
sentences.l:
and let not anyone, trusting in horsemanship and in manliness,
alone before the others be eager to fight with the Trojans,
sentences.i: and let no one, trusting in his horsemanship and his manliness, be eager to fight the Trojans alone in front of the others,
sentences.n: The infinitives give way to third-person commands, for Nestor’s orders are told as if spoken. μηδέ τις ‘and let no one’ is the subject; πεποιθώς ‘trusting’ (perfect participle of πείθομαι) takes the datives ἱπποσύνῃ ‘horsemanship’ and ἠνορέηφι ‘manliness’, the second in -φι. οἶος πρόσθ’ ἄλλων ‘alone in front of the others’ is the fault to be avoided. μεμάτω is the imperative of the perfect μέμαα ‘be eager’, and Τρώεσσι is the epic dative plural.

sentences.t: μηδ’ ἀναχωρείτω· ἀλαπαδνότεροι γὰρ ἔσεσθε.
sentences.l: nor let him step back; for feebler you will be.
sentences.i: and let him not step back either; for you will be the feebler.
sentences.n: μηδ’ ἀναχωρείτω is a second command with the same subject, ‘nor let him step back’ (present imperative of ἀναχωρέω). ἀλαπαδνότεροι ‘feebler’ is the comparative of ἀλαπαδνός ‘feeble’, and ἔσεσθε ‘you will be’ is second person plural: the report slips into Nestor’s own words, addressed to the horsemen.

sentences.t:
ὃς δέ κ’ ἀνὴρ ἀπὸ ὧν ὀχέων ἕτερ’ ἅρμαθ’ ἵκηται
ἔγχει ὀρεξάσθω,
sentences.l:
And whichever man from his own chariot reaches other chariots,
let him reach out with his spear,
sentences.i: And any man who from his own chariot comes up to other chariots, let him thrust with his spear,
sentences.n: ὃς δέ κ’ ἀνήρ ‘and whichever man’ is a relative clause with κε and the subjunctive ἵκηται ‘reaches’, so it is general, ‘any man who…’. ἀπὸ ὧν ὀχέων ‘from his own chariot’ uses ὅς as the possessive ‘his own’, and ἕτερ’ ἅρμαθ’ is ‘other chariots’ (ἅρματα elided, with θ for τ before the rough breathing of ἵκηται). ὀρεξάσθω is the aorist imperative middle of ὀρέγομαι ‘reach out’, and ἔγχει is the dative of ἔγχος ‘spear’: the man is to strike from his own chariot, not to leave it.

sentences.t: ἐπεὶ ἦ πολὺ φέρτερον οὕτω.
sentences.l: since truly much better it is thus.
sentences.i: since indeed it is far better so.
sentences.n: ἐπεί ‘since’ gives the reason for the thrust. ἦ ‘truly’ adds weight, φέρτερον is the comparative of φέρτερος ‘better, stronger’, and πολύ ‘by much’ strengthens it; ‘it is’ is left unsaid. οὕτω ‘thus’ points to fighting with the spear from the chariot instead of charging out alone. The line closes Nestor’s instructions to the horsemen.

sentences.t:
ὧδε καὶ οἱ πρότεροι πόλεας καὶ τείχε’ ἐπόρθεον
τόνδε νόον καὶ θυμὸν ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ἔχοντες.
sentences.l:
In this way also the men of before were sacking cities and walls,
having this mind and heart in their chests.
sentences.i: This was how the men of earlier days also sacked cities and walls, with this mind and heart in their breasts.
sentences.n: ὧδε … καί ‘in this way also’ points to the practice just described; οἱ πρότεροι ‘those before’ are men of earlier generations (the article as a pronoun). ἐπόρθεον is an imperfect of πορθέω ‘sack’ (related to πέρθω), for what they did again and again; πόλεας is the epic accusative plural of πόλις, and τείχε’ is τείχεα ‘walls’, elided. νόον and θυμόν are ‘mind’ and ‘heart’, and τόνδε ‘this’ goes with νόον: the same temper that Nestor asks of his men now.

sentences.t: ὣς ὃ γέρων ὄτρυνε πάλαι πολέμων ἐῢ εἰδώς·
sentences.l: So the old man urged on, long since knowing wars well;
sentences.i: So the old man urged them on, long well versed in war;
sentences.n: ὃ γέρων ‘the old man’ is ὁ used as a pronoun with its noun: Nestor. ὄτρυνε is an imperfect of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’, without augment. εἰδώς is the perfect participle of οἶδα ‘know’; with the genitive πολέμων it is ‘versed in war’, and ἐῢ ‘well’ and πάλαι ‘long since’ strengthen it. The line closes Nestor’s arrangement as 292 closed the visit to the Ajaxes. A new paragraph begins at 310.

sentences.t:
καὶ τὸν μὲν γήθησεν ἰδὼν κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων,
καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
And at him rejoiced, seeing, lord Agamemnon,
and, lifting his voice, to him winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: Lord Agamemnon rejoiced when he saw him, and lifting his voice he spoke winged words to him:
sentences.n: These are the two lines of 283–284, with τόν ‘him’ (Nestor) for τούς ‘them’ and μιν ‘him’ for σφεας ‘them’: the first rejoices at the sight, the second brings in the speech. γήθησεν ‘rejoiced’, ἰδών ‘seeing’ and κρείων ‘lord’ are as at 283. Line 312 also stands at 1.201, where μιν is Athena and the English says ‘to her’; here μιν is Nestor. ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα ‘he spoke winged words’ is the stock line.

sentences.t:
ὦ γέρον εἴθ’ ὡς θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσι φίλοισιν
ὥς τοι γούναθ’ ἕποιτο, βίη δέ τοι ἔμπεδος εἴη·
sentences.l:
“Old man, would that, as the heart in your dear chest,
so your knees might follow, and your might be firm;
sentences.i: “Old man, if only, as your heart is in your breast, your knees would follow it, and your might were firm;
sentences.n: ὦ γέρον ‘old man’ is a respectful vocative. εἴθε ‘if only’ opens a wish with two optatives, ἕποιτο ‘might follow’ and εἴη ‘might be’. ὡς … ὥς is ‘as … so’: as the heart is in the chest, so may the knees follow it. τοι is ‘your’ (a dative of the person concerned), γούναθ’ is γούνατα ‘knees’, and βίη ‘might’ with ἔμπεδος ‘firm’ adds a second wish. The thought is that Nestor’s spirit is willing but his body is not.

sentences.t: ἀλλά σε γῆρας τείρει ὁμοίϊον·
sentences.l: But old age wears you down, common to all;
sentences.i: But old age, which is the same for everyone, wears you down;
sentences.n: ἀλλά marks the turn from wish to fact: σε ‘you’ is the object of τείρει ‘wears down’ (τείρω), and γῆρας ‘old age’ is the subject. ὁμοίϊον agrees with γῆρας; it is a rare word built on ὅμοιος ‘alike’, and ‘common to all, the same for everyone’ is the usual sense, though how exactly Agamemnon means it is not certain. The unit ends at the stop in the middle of line 315.

sentences.t:
ὡς ὄφελέν τις
ἀνδρῶν ἄλλος ἔχειν, σὺ δὲ κουροτέροισι μετεῖναι.
sentences.l:
would that some
other of men had it, and you were among the younger.”
sentences.i: Would that some other man had it, and you were among the younger men.”
sentences.n: ὡς ὄφελε(ν) with an infinitive is a wish that cannot now come true, ‘would that…’ (ὄφελον is an old aorist of ὀφείλω ‘owe, ought’, fixed as a wish-word). τις ἀνδρῶν ἄλλος ‘some other of men’ is the one who should have old age, ἔχειν ‘to have it’ (the γῆρας of the last unit). σὺ δέ ‘and you’ is the person to be spared; κουροτέροισι is the dative of κουρότερος ‘younger’ (from κοῦρος ‘youth’), and μετεῖναι ‘to be among’ is the infinitive of μέτειμι. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ·
sentences.l: Him then answered the Gerenian horseman Nestor:
sentences.i: Then the Gerenian horseman Nestor answered him:
sentences.n: The reply formula, as in the Odyssey: τόν ‘him’ is Agamemnon, ἠμείβετο ‘answered’, ἔπειτα ‘then’. Nestor’s name-epithet is Γερήνιος ἱππότα, ‘the Gerenian horseman’: ἱππότα is an old nominative in -ᾱ (= ἱππότης), and the meaning of Γερήνιος is disputed (a place, Gerenia, or a word related to γέρων ‘old man’), so the English leaves it as a name. A new paragraph begins at 317.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδη μάλα μέν τοι ἐγὼν ἐθέλοιμι καὶ αὐτὸς
ὣς ἔμεν ὡς ὅτε δῖον Ἐρευθαλίωνα κατέκταν.
sentences.l:
“Atreus’-son, very much indeed would I myself too wish
to be so, as when heavenly Ereuthalion I killed.
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus, I myself too would very much like to be as I was when I killed heavenly Ereuthalion.
sentences.n: Ἀτρεΐδη is the vocative ‘son of Atreus’. μάλα μέν τοι ‘very much indeed’ stresses the wish, as at 266; ἐγών is the epic ἐγώ, and ἐθέλοιμι ‘I would wish’ an optative of what could be. καὶ αὐτός ‘I myself too’ joins Nestor’s wish to Agamemnon’s. ὣς ἔμεν ὡς ὅτε ‘to be as when’ uses the epic infinitive ἔμεν; κατέκταν is an aorist of κατακτείνω ‘kill’, here ‘I killed’ (the form could also be a third plural, but it is Nestor’s own deed). δῖον ‘heavenly’ goes with Ἐρευθαλίωνα, an Arcadian champion whom Nestor tells of at length in Book 7.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ οὔ πως ἅμα πάντα θεοὶ δόσαν ἀνθρώποισιν·
sentences.l: But in no way all things at once did the gods give to men;
sentences.i: But the gods do not give men everything at once;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ‘but’ turns from the wish to a common fact. οὔ πως means ‘in no way’, ἅμα ‘at once’ goes with πάντα ‘all things’, and δόσαν is the unaugmented aorist of δίδωμι (= ἔδοσαν), ‘gave’. The aorist here states what is always true, so English uses the present.

sentences.t: εἰ τότε κοῦρος ἔα νῦν αὖτέ με γῆρας ὀπάζει.
sentences.l: if then a youth I was, now in turn old age attends me.
sentences.i: If I was a young man then, now in its turn old age attends me.
sentences.n: εἰ τότε κοῦρος ἔα ‘if I was a youth then’ is the first half of a pair, and the second half follows without a link: νῦν αὖτέ με γῆρας ὀπάζει ‘now in turn old age attends me’. The ‘if’ grants the earlier time rather than doubting it. ἔα is the epic imperfect of εἰμί (= ἦν), and ὀπάζει is from ὀπάζω ‘make follow, attend’, with με ‘me’ as object: old age is now Nestor’s attendant. The pair is his example of the gods’ not giving everything at once.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ καὶ ὧς ἱππεῦσι μετέσσομαι ἠδὲ κελεύσω
βουλῇ καὶ μύθοισι·
sentences.l:
But even so I will be among the horsemen, and will give orders
with counsel and with words;
sentences.i: But even so I shall be among the horsemen and give them orders with counsel and with words;
sentences.n: καὶ ὧς ‘even so’ answers the complaint about age. μετέσσομαι is the future of μέτειμι ‘be among’, with the dative ἱππεῦσι ‘the horsemen’, and ἠδὲ κελεύσω ‘and I shall give orders’ adds the second thing he will do. βουλῇ and μύθοισι are datives of means, ‘by counsel’ and ‘by words’: what an old man can still give.

sentences.t: τὸ γὰρ γέρας ἐστὶ γερόντων.
sentences.l: for that is the prize of old men.
sentences.i: for that is the old men’s prize of honour.
sentences.n: τὸ γὰρ γέρας gives the reason: γέρας is the ‘prize of honour’, the share of respect that goes with rank (as at 1.118). The sound of γέρας and γερόντων ‘of old men’ is close, and the line sets the old man’s due, counsel and speech, against the young men’s spears in the next line.

sentences.t:
αἰχμὰς δ’ αἰχμάσσουσι νεώτεροι, οἵ περ ἐμεῖο
ὁπλότεροι γεγάασι πεποίθασίν τε βίηφιν.
sentences.l:
And spears will wield the younger men, who than I
are younger, and trust in their might.”
sentences.i: It is the younger men who will wield spears, those who are younger than I am and trust in their might.”
sentences.n: αἰχμὰς αἰχμάσσουσι is ‘they will wield spears’: αἰχμάσσουσι is a form of αἰχμάζω ‘wield the spear’ (the doubled σ is epic, and a future is the usual reading), and αἰχμάς ‘spears’ comes from the same root. νεώτεροι ‘younger men’ is the subject, picked up by οἵ περ … ὁπλότεροι γεγάασι ‘who are younger’: ἐμεῖο is the epic ἐμοῦ, the genitive of comparison, and γεγάασι is the perfect of γίγνομαι, ‘have been born’, so ‘are’. πεποίθασιν ‘they trust’ takes βίηφιν, an -φιν dative, ‘in their might’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, Ἀτρεΐδης δὲ παρῴχετο γηθόσυνος κῆρ.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and Atreus’-son went past, glad in heart.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the son of Atreus passed on, glad at heart.
sentences.n: The line repeats 272, except for the stop: ὣς ἔφατ’ now closes Nestor’s speech as it closed Idomeneus’ earlier, and Ἀτρεΐδης ‘son of Atreus’, Agamemnon, goes on again, γηθόσυνος κῆρ ‘glad in heart’ (κῆρ is an accusative of respect). παρῴχετο ‘went past’ is the imperfect of παροίχομαι. A new paragraph begins at 326.

sentences.t:
εὗρ’ υἱὸν Πετεῶο Μενεσθῆα πλήξιππον
ἑσταότ’·
sentences.l:
He found the son of Peteos, horse-lashing Menestheus,
standing;
sentences.i: He found Menestheus, son of Peteos, the horse-lasher, standing there;
sentences.n: εὗρ’ is εὗρε ‘he found’, the aorist of εὑρίσκω; the subject, Agamemnon, is left unsaid, and the line begins the next stop on his round. υἱὸν Πετεῶο Μενεσθῆα is ‘Menestheus, the son of Peteos’, with the epic genitive Πετεῶο (= Πετεῶ). πλήξιππον ‘horse-lashing’ is a compound of πλήσσω ‘strike’ and ἵππος, as at 2.104. ἑσταότ’ is the perfect participle of ἵστημι, ‘standing’, elided, and agrees with Μενεσθῆα.

sentences.t: ἀμφὶ δ’ Ἀθηναῖοι μήστωρες ἀϋτῆς·
sentences.l: and around, the Athenians, counsellors of the battle-cry;
sentences.i: and around him the Athenians, masters of the battle-cry;
sentences.n: ἀμφί is an adverb here, ‘around’, and a verb ‘stood’ is understood from ἑσταότ’. μήστωρες is from the root of μήδομαι ‘plan’, ‘counsellors’; with the genitive ἀϋτῆς ‘of the battle-cry’ it describes men expert in the fight, and the English gives it as ‘masters of the battle-cry’. Ἀθηναῖοι is ‘the Athenians’, Menestheus’ men.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ὃ πλησίον ἑστήκει πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς,
sentences.l: and he, nearby, was standing, many-wiled Odysseus,
sentences.i: and close by him stood Odysseus of many wiles,
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὅ is ‘and he’, with ὅ the old pronoun picking up the subject that follows, πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς; πολύμητις ‘of many wiles’ is his stock epithet, from μῆτις ‘cunning’. ἑστήκει is the pluperfect of ἵστημι, ‘was standing’, and πλησίον is the adverb ‘near’: Odysseus is next to Menestheus.

sentences.t:
πὰρ δὲ Κεφαλλήνων ἀμφὶ στίχες οὐκ ἀλαπαδναὶ
ἕστασαν·
sentences.l:
and beside, around, of the Cephallenians the ranks, not feeble,
stood;
sentences.i: and beside him, round about, stood the ranks of the Cephallenians, no feeble ones;
sentences.n: πάρ (= παρά) and ἀμφί are both adverbs, ‘beside’ and ‘around’, and ἕστασαν ‘stood’ (the plural of the pluperfect, as ἑστήκει above) is the verb; στίχες Κεφαλλήνων is ‘the ranks of the Cephallenians’, Odysseus’ own men. οὐκ ἀλαπαδναί ‘not feeble’ is a litotes: ‘not weak’ for ‘strong’. ἀλαπαδνός ‘feeble’ returns at 305.

sentences.t: οὐ γάρ πώ σφιν ἀκούετο λαὸς ἀϋτῆς,
sentences.l: for not yet were their people hearing the battle-cry,
sentences.i: for their troops had not yet heard the battle-cry,
sentences.n: The reason follows: οὐ γάρ πώ ‘for not yet’. σφιν is the dative of the pronoun, ‘to them’, used as ‘their’ with λαός ‘people, army’; ἀκούετο is the imperfect middle of ἀκούω ‘hear’, here with active sense, ‘was hearing’, and the genitive ἀϋτῆς ‘of the battle-cry’ is what is heard. So the Cephallenians had not yet heard the shout that starts the fighting.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ νέον συνορινόμεναι κίνυντο φάλαγγες
Τρώων ἱπποδάμων καὶ Ἀχαιῶν·
sentences.l:
but newly, stirring together, were moving the battle-lines
of the horse-taming Trojans and of the Achaeans;
sentences.i: but the battle-lines of the Trojans, tamers of horses, and of the Achaeans were only just stirring into motion together;
sentences.n: ἀλλά ‘but’ gives the other side: νέον ‘newly, just now’ goes with συνορινόμεναι ‘being stirred together’ (a middle or passive participle of συνορίνω ‘stir up together’), and κίνυντο ‘were moving’ is the imperfect middle of κίνυμαι, the verb used of the ranks at 281. φάλαγγες ‘battle-lines’ is the subject; Τρώων ἱπποδάμων ‘of the horse-taming Trojans’ and Ἀχαιῶν are genitives that depend on it.

sentences.t:
οἳ δὲ μένοντες
ἕστασαν ὁππότε πύργος Ἀχαιῶν ἄλλος ἐπελθὼν
Τρώων ὁρμήσειε καὶ ἄρξειαν πολέμοιο.
sentences.l:
and they, waiting,
stood until the time when another tower of the Achaeans, coming on,
should rush at the Trojans, and they should begin the war.
sentences.i: and they stood waiting for the moment when another tower of the Achaeans would advance and rush at the Trojans, and they would begin the war.
sentences.n: οἳ δέ ‘and they’ are the waiting men, the Athenians and Cephallenians; μένοντες ‘waiting’ and ἕστασαν ‘stood’ go together. ὁππότε with the optatives ὁρμήσειε and ἄρξειαν gives the moment awaited, ‘until the time when’, after a past main verb. πύργος Ἀχαιῶν ἄλλος ‘another tower of the Achaeans’ is a close-packed body of men seen as a tower, and ἐπελθών ‘coming on’ agrees with it; Τρώων ὁρμήσειε ‘should rush at the Trojans’ takes the genitive of what is attacked. The subject of the plural ἄρξειαν ‘they should begin’ (πολέμοιο ‘the war’ in the genitive) is not stated: it may be the waiting men or the Achaeans in general.

sentences.t:
τοὺς δὲ ἰδὼν νείκεσσεν ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων,
καί σφεας φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
And them seeing, reviled them the lord of men Agamemnon,
and, lifting his voice, to them winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: When he saw them, Agamemnon, lord of men, reviled them, and lifting his voice he spoke winged words to them:
sentences.n: Agamemnon sees the two groups standing still and rebukes them. τοὺς δὲ ἰδών ‘and seeing them’ takes the old pronoun τούς; νείκεσσεν is the aorist of νεικέω ‘revile’, with the epic -σσ-, and ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν ‘lord of men’ is Agamemnon’s stock title. The second line is the stock line of 284: σφεας ‘them’, φωνήσας ‘lifting his voice’, ἔπεα πτερόεντα ‘winged words’, προσηύδα ‘he spoke to’.

sentences.l:
“O son of Peteos, the Zeus-nurtured king,
and you, outstanding in evil tricks, gain-minded one,
why, cowering, do you stand aloof, and wait for others?
sentences.i: “Son of Peteos, the Zeus-nurtured king, and you, who excel in evil tricks, with your mind on gain — why do you cower and hold aloof, and wait for others?
sentences.n: Two men are addressed. The first vocative, ὦ υἱὲ Πετεῶο, is Menestheus, and καὶ σύ ‘and you’, with κεκασμένε and κερδαλεόφρον, turns to Odysseus, who answers at 349. διοτρεφέος βασιλῆος ‘Zeus-nurtured king’ is Peteos. κεκασμένε is the perfect passive participle of καίνυμαι ‘excel’, with the dative κακοῖσι δόλοισι ‘in evil tricks’; κερδαλεόφρον ‘gain-minded’ is a sharp word. The question has plural verbs: καταπτώσσοντες ‘cowering’, ἀφέστατε ‘you stand aloof’ (perfect of ἀφίστημι), and μίμνετε, the epic form of μένετε, with ἄλλους ‘others’ as what they wait for. The line is metrically irregular as transmitted: the short final syllable of υἱέ stands where the second foot needs a long one.

sentences.t:
σφῶϊν μέν τ’ ἐπέοικε μετὰ πρώτοισιν ἐόντας
ἑστάμεν ἠδὲ μάχης καυστείρης ἀντιβολῆσαι·
sentences.l:
To you two indeed it is fitting, being among the foremost,
to stand, and to encounter the burning battle;
sentences.i: It is fitting for you two to stand among the foremost and to meet the burning battle;
sentences.n: σφῶϊν is the dual dative ‘to you two’ (Menestheus and Odysseus), and μέν τε ‘indeed’ looks ahead to νῦν δέ in 347, which sets the present against what is fitting. ἐπέοικε ‘it is fitting’ governs two infinitives, ἑστάμεν (epic for ἑστάναι) ‘to stand’ and ἀντιβολῆσαι ‘to meet’, which takes the genitive; ἐόντας ‘being’ is an accusative plural participle that agrees with the unspoken ‘you’. μετὰ πρώτοισιν is ‘among the foremost’, and μάχης καυστείρης ‘burning battle’ uses a rare word from the root of καίω ‘burn’.

sentences.t:
πρώτω γὰρ καὶ δαιτὸς ἀκουάζεσθον ἐμεῖο,
ὁππότε δαῖτα γέρουσιν ἐφοπλίζωμεν Ἀχαιοί.
sentences.l:
for you two, first, also hear of my feast,
whenever we Achaeans prepare a feast for the elders.
sentences.i: for you two are the first to hear of my feast as well, whenever we Achaeans prepare a feast for the elders.
sentences.n: πρώτω ‘first’ is dual, agreeing with the two addressed. καί ‘also’ links the feast to the battle line: first in the fight, and first at the feast too. ἀκουάζεσθον is the dual of ἀκουάζομαι, a rare word for ‘listen, hear’ (here ‘be told of’), with the genitive δαιτός ‘feast’; ἐμεῖο is the epic ἐμοῦ ‘my’. ὁππότε with the subjunctive ἐφοπλίζωμεν ‘we prepare’ makes it general, ‘whenever’; γέρουσιν is the dative of γέρων, ‘for the elders’, the leaders honoured at the feast (compare 259–262).

sentences.t:
ἔνθα φίλ’ ὀπταλέα κρέα ἔδμεναι ἠδὲ κύπελλα
οἴνου πινέμεναι μελιηδέος ὄφρ’ ἐθέλητον·
sentences.l:
There dear roast meats to eat, and cups
of honey-sweet wine to drink, as long as you two wish;
sentences.i: There are roast meats you love to eat, and cups of honey-sweet wine to drink, for as long as you wish;
sentences.n: ἔνθα ‘there’ is the feast. φίλ’ is φίλα ‘dear, welcome’, going with ὀπταλέα κρέα ‘roast meats’ (ὀπταλέος is from ὀπτάω ‘roast’), and the infinitives ἔδμεναι ‘to eat’ and πινέμεναι ‘to drink’ are the epic forms in -μεναι, saying what the meats and cups are for; no verb ‘is’ is needed. κύπελλα are cups, and οἴνου μελιηδέος is ‘of honey-sweet wine’, a genitive of what fills them. ὄφρ’ ἐθέλητον ‘as long as you two wish’ has a dual subjunctive.

sentences.t:
νῦν δὲ φίλως χ’ ὁρόῳτε καὶ εἰ δέκα πύργοι Ἀχαιῶν
ὑμείων προπάροιθε μαχοίατο νηλέϊ χαλκῷ.
sentences.l:
but now gladly you would look on, even if ten towers of the Achaeans
in front of you were fighting with pitiless bronze.”
sentences.i: but now you would gladly look on, even if ten towers of the Achaeans were fighting with pitiless bronze in front of you.”
sentences.n: νῦν δέ ‘but now’ turns from the feast to the present. χ’ is κε, with the optative ὁρόῳτε (ὁράω in its epic form, here second person plural, though the duals of 341–346 have addressed only the two) for what they would do, and φίλως ‘gladly’ is the sting: they would watch with pleasure. καὶ εἰ ‘even if’ takes the optative μαχοίατο ‘should fight’; δέκα πύργοι Ἀχαιῶν ‘ten towers of the Achaeans’ means ten close-packed bodies of men (as at 334). ὑμείων is the epic ὑμῶν, and προπάροιθε ‘in front of’ governs it; νηλέϊ χαλκῷ ‘pitiless bronze’ stands for the weapons. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπόδρα ἰδὼν προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l: Him then with a scowl looking addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: Then Odysseus of many wiles, looking at him with a scowl, spoke to him:
sentences.n: Odysseus answers: τόν ‘him’ is Agamemnon, and δ’ ἄρ’ is ‘and then’. ὑπόδρα ἰδών ‘looking with a scowl’ is the stock look of anger or reproach; the ancient explanation of ὑπόδρα is ‘from under the brows’, but the derivation is not certain. προσέφη ‘addressed’ and πολύμητις ‘of many wiles’ are as at 329. A new paragraph begins at 349.

sentences.t: Ἀτρεΐδη ποῖόν σε ἔπος φύγεν ἕρκος ὀδόντων;
sentences.l: “Atreus’-son, what sort of word has escaped you, (past) the fence of your teeth?
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus, what kind of word has slipped past the fence of your teeth?
sentences.n: Odysseus’ answer opens with a vocative, Ἀτρεΐδη ‘son of Atreus’, and a question that is a charge. ποῖον ‘what sort of’ goes with ἔπος ‘word’, and φύγεν is ἔφυγε, an unaugmented aorist of φεύγω ‘flee, escape’: σε ‘you’ is its object, and ἕρκος ὀδόντων ‘the fence of the teeth’ is what the word passes. The image of the teeth as a fence is Homer’s own, and it recurs in the Odyssey; the English keeps it.

sentences.t:
πῶς δὴ φῂς πολέμοιο μεθιέμεν ὁππότ’ Ἀχαιοὶ
Τρωσὶν ἐφ’ ἱπποδάμοισιν ἐγείρομεν ὀξὺν Ἄρηα;
sentences.l:
How, then, do you say that we slacken from war, when we Achaeans
against the horse-taming Trojans rouse sharp Ares?
sentences.i: How, then, do you say that we are slack in war, when we Achaeans are rousing keen battle against the Trojans, tamers of horses?
sentences.n: πῶς δή ‘how then’ opens a challenge to what Agamemnon said. φῂς is φῄς ‘you say’ (2nd singular of φημί), with the infinitive μεθιέμεν (= μεθιέναι) ‘to slacken’, which takes the genitive πολέμοιο ‘from war’ or ‘in war’. ὁππότ’ ‘when’ has ἐγείρομεν ‘we rouse’. ὀξὺν Ἄρηα ‘sharp Ares’ is the war-god put for war itself; ἐπί with the dative Τρωσίν gives ‘against the Trojans’, and ἱπποδάμοισιν ‘tamers of horses’ is their stock epithet.

sentences.t:
ὄψεαι αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃσθα καὶ αἴ κέν τοι τὰ μεμήλῃ
Τηλεμάχοιο φίλον πατέρα προμάχοισι μιγέντα
Τρώων ἱπποδάμων·
sentences.i: You will see, if you wish, and if these things concern you, Telemachus’ dear father mingled with the foremost fighters of the Trojans, tamers of horses;
sentences.n: Odysseus speaks of himself in the third person, as Τηλεμάχοιο φίλον πατέρα ‘the dear father of Telemachus’. ὄψεαι ‘you will see’ is the future middle of ὁράω; αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃσθα and αἴ κέν τοι τὰ μεμήλῃ are two conditions, ‘if you wish’ and ‘if these things concern you’ (μεμήλῃ is the perfect subjunctive of μέλω ‘be a care’, and τά ‘these things’ the matters of war). μιγέντα, the aorist passive participle of μίγνυμι, ‘mingled’, agrees with πατέρα and takes the dative προμάχοισι ‘front-fighters’; Τρώων ἱπποδάμων ‘of the horse-taming Trojans’ depends on them.

sentences.t: σὺ δὲ ταῦτ’ ἀνεμώλια βάζεις.
sentences.l: but you speak these things, empty ones.”
sentences.i: but you talk this empty nonsense.”
sentences.n: σὺ δέ ‘but you’ sets Agamemnon against the picture of Odysseus in the fighting. ταῦτ’ is ταῦτα ‘these things’, the object of βάζεις ‘you speak’, and ἀνεμώλια ‘empty’ (formed from ἄνεμος ‘wind’, so ‘windy’) agrees with it: the words are like wind. Agamemnon will use a like word of his own speech at 363, μεταμώνια. Odysseus’ speech ends here.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ἐπιμειδήσας προσέφη κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων
ὡς γνῶ χωομένοιο·
sentences.l:
Him then smiling at addressed lord Agamemnon,
when he knew him incensed;
sentences.i: Then lord Agamemnon, smiling at him, spoke to him when he saw that he was incensed;
sentences.n: This is the frame of the Odyssey’s τὸν δ’ ἐπιμειδήσας προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς, with κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων for the speaker: ἐπιμειδήσας is the aorist participle of ἐπιμειδάω ‘smile at’. ὡς γνῶ ‘when he knew’ (γνῶ = ἔγνω, aorist of γιγνώσκω) takes the genitive participle χωομένοιο ‘incensed’ (from χώομαι), agreeing with the unnamed ‘him’, Odysseus. The smile is followed at once by Agamemnon’s taking back what he said. A new paragraph begins at 356.

sentences.t: πάλιν δ’ ὅ γε λάζετο μῦθον·
sentences.l: and back he took his word:
sentences.i: and he took back his word:
sentences.n: λάζετο is the imperfect middle of λάζομαι ‘take, seize’, and πάλιν ‘back’ goes with it: he took back his word, μῦθον. ὅ γε ‘he for his part’ contrasts with the angry Odysseus. The imperfect fits what follows, since the speech of 358–363 is the taking back.

sentences.t:
διογενὲς Λαερτιάδη πολυμήχαν’ Ὀδυσσεῦ
οὔτέ σε νεικείω περιώσιον οὔτε κελεύω·
sentences.l:
“Zeus-sprung son of Laertes, many-devising Odysseus,
neither do I revile you excessively nor do I order you;
sentences.i: “Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus, man of many devices, I do not revile you unduly, nor do I give you orders;
sentences.n: The vocative is the stock one for Odysseus, as at 2.173: διογενές ‘Zeus-sprung’, Λαερτιάδη ‘son of Laertes’ and πολυμήχαν’ (πολυμήχανε) ‘of many devices’. οὔτε … οὔτε ‘neither … nor’ governs νεικείω (νεικέω with the epic spelling) ‘I revile’ and κελεύω ‘I order’, each with σε ‘you’; περιώσιον ‘beyond measure’ goes with the first. Agamemnon withdraws both the reproach and the orders implied in his rebuke.

sentences.t:
οἶδα γὰρ ὥς τοι θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσι φίλοισιν
ἤπια δήνεα οἶδε·
sentences.l:
for I know how your heart in your dear chest
knows kindly designs;
sentences.i: for I know that the heart in your breast is kindly in its designs;
sentences.n: οἶδα γάρ explains the retraction: ‘for I know…’. ὥς τοι here is ‘how, that’ (the conjunction ὡς) with τοι ‘your’; θυμός ‘heart’ is the subject, and οἶδε ‘knows’ has ἤπια δήνεα ‘kindly designs’ as its object. To ‘know kindly designs’ is to be kindly disposed, as in the Odyssey’s ἤπια οἶδε. δήνεα is a poetic word for ‘plans, counsels’, and ἤπια ‘kindly’ is the neuter plural of ἤπιος.

sentences.t: τὰ γὰρ φρονέεις ἅ τ’ ἐγώ περ.
sentences.l: for you think the things that I too think.
sentences.i: for you think just what I think.
sentences.n: τὰ γάρ ‘for those things’ gives the reason for his trust. φρονέεις is the second person of φρονέω ‘think, have in mind’ (uncontracted -εεις), and ἅ τ’ ἐγώ περ ‘the things that I myself’ leaves the verb ‘think’ to be understood; τε and περ are particles that stress the likeness. Odysseus and Agamemnon are of one mind.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἴθι ταῦτα δ’ ὄπισθεν ἀρεσσόμεθ’ εἴ τι κακὸν νῦν
εἴρηται,
sentences.l:
But go on; these things afterwards we will put right, if anything bad now
has been said,
sentences.i: But go on; we shall put these things right later, if anything bad has been said now,
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἴθι ‘but go on’ is the imperative of εἶμι ‘go’. ταῦτα ‘these things’ is the object of ἀρεσσόμεθ’, a future middle of ἀρέσκω, here ‘make good, put right’, with ὄπισθεν ‘afterwards’. εἴ τι κακὸν νῦν εἴρηται is the condition, ‘if anything bad has now been said’, where εἴρηται is the perfect passive of the verb whose future is ἐρῶ. The comma after it ends the unit; the wish that follows depends on it.

sentences.t: τὰ δὲ πάντα θεοὶ μεταμώνια θεῖεν.
sentences.l: and all those things may the gods make empty.”
sentences.i: and may the gods make all of it empty.”
sentences.n: τὰ … πάντα ‘all those things’ are the hasty words, the object of θεῖεν, the aorist optative of τίθημι, in a wish: ‘may the gods make…’; μεταμώνια ‘empty’ is what they are to be made. The word is built, it is usually said, from μετά and ἄνεμος ‘wind’, so ‘windy’, and it is used of idle talk elsewhere. Agamemnon’s speech ends here.
